claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability is governed primarily by entropy-driven stabilization of the solid-solution phase.
Entropy-driven stabilization suppresses phase segregation up to a critical temperature.
Entropy-driven stabilization suppresses elemental diffusion up to a critical temperature.
High-melting-point, low-diffusivity elements act as anchors within the nanoparticle lattice.
W, Mo, and Ta are examples of high-melting-point, low-diffusivity elements suitable for the proposed intervention.
Systematically including or excluding W, Mo, or Ta while retaining near-equiatomic ratios will isolate the proposed anchoring effect.
High configurational entropy in near-equiatomic compositions stabilizes the solid solution against phase segregation.
Adding high-melting-point, low-diffusivity elements reduces atomic mobility.
Reduced atomic mobility delays or prevents phase separation and chemical instability during high-temperature service.
Nanoparticles containing high-melting-point, low-diffusivity elements will undergo less phase segregation than nanoparticles lacking those elements.
Nanoparticles containing high-melting-point, low-diffusivity elements will better maintain elemental composition and crystallinity during high-temperature exposure.
The stabilizing effect of high-melting-point, low-diffusivity elements will be most pronounced near the upper end of the service-temperature range.
Near-equiatomic nanoparticles lacking high-melting-point, low-diffusivity elements are expected to show more phase segregation and elemental diffusion under identical conditions.
The hypothesis applies to near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles containing at least four elements.
The hypothesis applies only at service temperatures below the melting point of the lowest-melting constituent.
The hypothesis does not apply to significantly compositionally imbalanced nanoparticles.
The hypothesis does not apply in highly reactive atmospheres that cause rapid surface reactions.
Equal or greater stability in the nanoparticles lacking the proposed anchor elements at 1173 K would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions present 473–1923 K as the thermoelectric exposure regime, whereas the boundary limits applicability to temperatures below the melting point of the lowest-melting constituent. Depending on composition, this can exclude part of the stated range, especially its upper end.
The effect is predicted to be most pronounced near the upper end of the service-temperature range, but the hypothesis may cease to apply before that upper end if the lowest-melting constituent melts.
